title: 3-Read Friday #49: Praise, Do Nows, and Working Memory
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue draws together coaching technique, Do Now design, and cognitive science, and Barton opens by disclosing his own recent shift in coaching practice. He describes how, over the past year, he has changed how he uses praise with teachers, prompting them to explain why they did something well rather than just naming the success, and credits Sarah Cottinghatt's post with articulating why that shift matters for surfacing a teacher's mental models. He then turns to Blake Harvard's five reasons for running a standalone retrieval Do Now, noting it echoes his own stated preference for Do Nows disconnected from the rest of the lesson. He closes with Dylan Kane's overview of working memory, praising it as an efficient explainer of a concept that has become common parlance among teachers thanks to Dan Willingham's influence.
points: Barton discloses a concrete change to his own coaching practice: prompting teachers to explain why a good action worked, not just praising the outcome.
He explicitly links Cottinghatt's framing to cognitive engagement, arguing that explaining reasoning engages teachers from the first minute of a coaching session.
He notes his own prior stated preference for standalone Do Nows, positioning Harvard's five reasons as validation of a position he already holds.
He credits Dan Willingham's broader influence for making 'working memory' common classroom parlance, framing Kane's post as an efficient way into that literature.
quotes: One of the biggest changes I have made to my coaching over the last 12 months has been how I present praise.

Prompting teachers to explain exactly why they do the good things that they do reveals important information about the strength of their mental models and gets them cognitively engaged in the coaching session from the first minute.
As I discuss here, I am a big fan of a standalone retrieval, Do Now, whose content is disconnected from the rest of the lesson.
Blake shares five reasons why his Do Nows follow a similar format.
Thanks to the work of Dan Willingham, and others, working memory is a term in most teachers' parlance.
Here, Dylan gives an efficient overview, a nice demonstration of working memory limitations, and examines the implications for the classroom.
